questions.question_text: Which of the following best defines chronic hypertension in pregnancy?

choices.text: Hypertension diagnosed before pregnancy or before 20 weeks of gestation
Hypertension that develops only during the second stage of labour
Hypertension that occurs exclusively after delivery
A temporary increase in blood pressure during fetal movement

questions.rationale: Chronic hypertension is hypertension that predates pregnancy or is identified before 20 weeks of gestation. It requires monitoring because it increases the risk of superimposed pre-eclampsia and adverse maternal and fetal outcomes.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 31 weeks presents with a blood pressure of 168/112 mmHg, severe headache and blurred vision. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

choices.text: Advise her to rest at home and return after one week
Arrange urgent obstetric assessment, initiate appropriate emergency care and monitor maternal and fetal wellbeing
Encourage unrestricted salt intake
Reassure her that elevated blood pressure is normal in late pregnancy

questions.rationale: Severe-range blood pressure with neurological symptoms suggests severe pre-eclampsia and a risk of eclampsia or stroke. Immediate assessment, treatment of severe hypertension, seizure prevention and fetal monitoring are required.

questions.question_text: Which medication is commonly used for seizure prevention in a woman with severe pre-eclampsia?

choices.text: Oxytocin
Ferrous sulphate
Magnesium sulphate
Metformin

questions.rationale: Magnesium sulphate is the recommended first-line anticonvulsant for preventing and treating eclamptic seizures. The midwife must monitor respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes and urine output during administration.

questions.question_text: A woman at 35 weeks' gestation with pre-eclampsia develops severe epigastric pain, nausea and a platelet count of 75,000/mm³. Which complication should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: HELLP syndrome
Gestational diabetes mellitus
Uncomplicated iron-deficiency anaemia
Physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux

questions.rationale: HELLP syndrome is characterised by haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelet count. Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain may indicate hepatic involvement and requires urgent obstetric management.

questions.question_text: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia suddenly develops a generalised seizure. What should the midwife prioritise?

choices.text: Insert a spoon into her mouth to prevent tongue biting
Restrain her limbs firmly
Give oral fluids immediately
Protect her from injury, maintain airway and breathing, and summon emergency assistance

questions.rationale: Eclampsia is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate protection from injury and support of airway and breathing. Magnesium sulphate and further maternal stabilisation should be provided according to the emergency protocol.

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes gestational diabetes mellitus?

choices.text: Diabetes that occurs only after the menopause
Hyperglycaemia first recognised during pregnancy that does not clearly meet criteria for overt diabetes in pregnancy
A condition caused exclusively by excessive sugar consumption during labour
A form of diabetes that always disappears before delivery

questions.rationale: Gestational diabetes mellitus is hyperglycaemia first recognised during pregnancy that does not meet the diagnostic criteria for overt diabetes. It is associated with maternal and fetal complications and requires appropriate screening and management.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman diagnosed with gestational diabetes is attending antenatal clinic. Which advice is most appropriate?

choices.text: Stop eating carbohydrates completely
Avoid all physical activity until delivery
Follow an individualised nutritional plan, undertake suitable physical activity and monitor blood glucose as advised
Discontinue antenatal visits because the condition is temporary

questions.rationale: Initial management commonly includes individualised medical nutrition therapy, appropriate physical activity and blood glucose monitoring. Medication such as insulin may be required when glycaemic targets are not achieved through lifestyle measures.

questions.question_text: A woman with gestational diabetes is admitted in labour. Her newborn is at increased risk of which immediate complication?

choices.text: Neonatal hypoglycaemia
Congenital absence of the kidneys in every case
Neonatal hyperthyroidism in every case
Permanent neonatal hypertension

questions.rationale: Maternal hyperglycaemia can stimulate fetal insulin production, which may persist after birth and cause neonatal hypoglycaemia. The newborn should receive appropriate early feeding and blood glucose monitoring according to the neonatal protocol.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with diabetes becomes sweaty, tremulous and confused. Her capillary blood glucose is 2.4 mmol/L. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Administer her usual insulin dose immediately
Encourage her to undertake physical exercise
Withhold all treatment until the next meal
Treat hypoglycaemia promptly according to protocol and reassess blood glucose

questions.rationale: A blood glucose level of 2.4 mmol/L with sweating and confusion indicates clinically significant hypoglycaemia. If the woman is conscious and able to swallow safely, fast-acting oral glucose should be given; if consciousness or swallowing is impaired, emergency treatment with appropriate intravenous glucose or glucagon should follow protocol.

questions.question_text: Which type of anaemia is most commonly associated with nutritional deficiency during pregnancy?

choices.text: Iron-deficiency anaemia
Aplastic anaemia
Haemolytic anaemia caused by autoimmune disease
Pernicious anaemia in every pregnant woman

questions.rationale: Iron-deficiency anaemia is a common nutritional problem during pregnancy because maternal iron requirements increase. It can be prevented or treated through appropriate dietary measures, iron supplementation and investigation of the underlying cause.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks presents with severe pallor, fatigue, breathlessness at rest and a haemoglobin level of 6.2 g/dL. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Advise her to increase fruit intake and return after one month
Recognise severe anaemia, arrange urgent clinical assessment and initiate appropriate management
Reassure her that low haemoglobin is expected in all pregnancies
Stop all antenatal investigations

questions.rationale: A haemoglobin level of 6.2 g/dL with breathlessness at rest indicates severe anaemia and possible cardiovascular compromise. Urgent assessment is necessary to determine the cause and the need for specialist treatment, including transfusion when clinically indicated.

questions.question_text: Which cardiac change normally occurs during pregnancy?

choices.text: A complete cessation of maternal cardiac activity
A reduction in circulating blood volume
An increase in cardiac output
A permanent reduction in heart rate below the normal range

questions.rationale: Cardiac output increases during pregnancy because of increased stroke volume and heart rate. These physiological adaptations support the increased metabolic and circulatory demands of the mother and fetus.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with known rheumatic heart disease presents with increasing breathlessness, orthopnoea and bilateral basal lung crepitations. What should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Normal physiological changes of pregnancy
Uncomplicated iron-deficiency anaemia
Normal fetal descent
Cardiac decompensation with possible pulmonary oedema

questions.rationale: Orthopnoea and pulmonary crepitations suggest pulmonary congestion and possible heart failure. The woman requires urgent assessment, oxygenation and specialist management to prevent maternal and fetal deterioration.

questions.question_text: A woman with known cardiac disease is in labour and becomes acutely breathless with oxygen saturation of 86%. What is the priority action?

choices.text: Position her appropriately, support oxygenation and urgently escalate for medical and obstetric review
Encourage her to push forcefully
Give unrestricted intravenous fluids
Delay assessment until after delivery

questions.rationale: Acute hypoxaemia and breathlessness in a woman with cardiac disease may indicate life-threatening cardiac decompensation. Airway and breathing support, careful fluid management and urgent specialist intervention are essential.

questions.question_text: Which blood pressure reading meets the threshold for severe hypertension in pregnancy?

choices.text: 130/80 mmHg
140/90 mmHg
160/110 mmHg or higher in either systolic or diastolic component
120/70 mmHg

questions.rationale: Severe hypertension in pregnancy is generally defined by systolic blood pressure of at least 160 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of at least 110 mmHg. It requires prompt confirmation and urgent treatment because of the risk of stroke and other complications.

questions.question_text: Which parasite causes malaria in humans?

choices.text: Trypanosoma brucei
Plasmodium species
Entamoeba histolytica
Leishmania donovani

questions.rationale: Malaria is caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium and transmitted through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. Plasmodium falciparum is the predominant cause of severe malaria in Ghana.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 26 weeks presents with fever, chills, headache and vomiting. Malaria is suspected. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Diagnose malaria based on symptoms alone and give any available antimalarial
Advise her to use mosquito repellent and return in one week
Assess severity, arrange prompt malaria testing and initiate appropriate treatment according to national guidelines
Withhold all investigations until after delivery

questions.rationale: Malaria in pregnancy can cause maternal anaemia, severe illness and adverse fetal outcomes. Prompt parasitological testing and treatment based on disease severity and current national guidance are essential.

questions.question_text: Which preventive intervention is recommended for eligible pregnant women in malaria-endemic areas of Ghana?

choices.text: Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, beginning in the second trimester according to national guidance
Routine daily treatment with artemisinin-based combination therapy throughout pregnancy
Avoidance of all insecticide-treated nets
Administration of antibiotics to every pregnant woman

questions.rationale: Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is recommended in eligible women in malaria-endemic settings, alongside insecticide-treated nets. It should begin in the second trimester and be administered at eligible antenatal contacts according to national policy.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with malaria develops altered consciousness, repeated vomiting and severe weakness. What should the midwife prioritise?

choices.text: Arrange routine outpatient review
Provide only oral fluids and discharge her
Delay treatment until the next antenatal clinic
Recognise possible severe malaria and arrange immediate emergency treatment and referral

questions.rationale: Altered consciousness and persistent vomiting are danger signs that may indicate severe malaria or another life-threatening condition. The woman requires urgent hospital management, parenteral antimalarial treatment when indicated and supportive care.

questions.question_text: Which intervention is central to preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV?

choices.text: Avoiding all antenatal HIV testing
Providing lifelong antiretroviral therapy to pregnant women living with HIV and supporting appropriate infant prophylaxis and follow-up
Stopping antiretroviral treatment once pregnancy is confirmed
Delaying all HIV-related care until after breastfeeding

questions.rationale: Effective antiretroviral therapy reduces maternal viral load and substantially lowers the risk of vertical HIV transmission. Appropriate infant prophylaxis, early infant diagnosis and adherence support are also important components of prevention.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman newly diagnosed with HIV asks whether she should begin antiretroviral therapy. What is the best response?

choices.text: Treatment should be delayed until the baby is delivered
Antiretroviral therapy is required only when symptoms develop
She should be linked promptly to HIV care and started on recommended lifelong antiretroviral therapy
She should stop attending antenatal clinic to avoid disclosure

questions.rationale: All pregnant women living with HIV should be promptly linked to treatment services and receive recommended antiretroviral therapy. Early and sustained treatment protects maternal health and reduces the risk of transmission to the infant.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman living with HIV has a detectable viral load close to delivery despite reporting adherence to treatment. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Ignore the result because viral load does not affect transmission risk
Stop all antiretroviral medicines immediately
Recommend that the woman avoid all facility-based delivery care
Escalate for specialist review, assess adherence and follow the prevention-of-vertical-transmission delivery and infant-care protocol

questions.rationale: A detectable viral load near delivery requires careful assessment because the risk of vertical transmission may be increased. The care team should review adherence and treatment history and plan delivery and infant prophylaxis according to current national guidance.

questions.question_text: Which laboratory test is commonly used for initial screening of hepatitis B infection in pregnancy?

choices.text: Hepatitis B surface antigen test
Mantoux test
Widal test
Random blood glucose test

questions.rationale: Hepatitis B surface antigen testing is used to identify current hepatitis B infection. A positive result requires further assessment and planning to reduce the risk of transmission to the newborn.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman tests positive for hepatitis B surface antigen. Which intervention is essential to reduce transmission to her newborn?

choices.text: Delay all newborn immunisation until six months of age
Give the newborn hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin promptly after birth when indicated and available under national guidance
Administer maternal antibiotics during labour as the only preventive measure
Avoid testing the newborn after delivery

questions.rationale: Timely hepatitis B vaccination, with hepatitis B immunoglobulin for infants of mothers who are hepatitis B surface antigen positive when indicated and available, reduces perinatal transmission. The newborn should complete the recommended immunisation schedule and receive appropriate follow-up.

questions.question_text: Which organism causes syphilis?

choices.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Chlamydia trachomatis
Treponema pallidum
Mycobacterium tuberculosis

questions.rationale: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the spirochaete bacterium Treponema pallidum. Untreated maternal infection can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, congenital syphilis and other adverse pregnancy outcomes.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman tests positive for syphilis during antenatal screening. Which treatment is recommended for preventing congenital syphilis?

choices.text: Oral metronidazole alone
Oral amoxicillin for three days
Topical antifungal cream
Appropriate penicillin treatment according to the stage of syphilis and national guidelines

questions.rationale: Penicillin is the recommended treatment for syphilis in pregnancy and is effective in preventing congenital infection when administered appropriately. The stage of infection determines the regimen, and partner evaluation and follow-up are also important.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with untreated syphilis delivers a stillborn infant. Which complication is most strongly associated with untreated maternal syphilis?

choices.text: Congenital syphilis
Congenital malaria in every case
Neonatal asthma
Congenital appendicitis

questions.rationale: Untreated maternal syphilis can cross the placenta and cause fetal infection, stillbirth, neonatal death and congenital syphilis. Antenatal screening and timely penicillin treatment are important maternal mortality and perinatal mortality reduction strategies.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman presents with a persistent cough, night sweats, weight loss and haemoptysis. What condition should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Uncomplicated allergic rhinitis
Pulmonary tuberculosis
Gestational diabetes
Iron-deficiency anaemia alone

questions.rationale: Persistent cough, night sweats, weight loss and haemoptysis are suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis. Prompt investigation, infection prevention measures and linkage to TB services are necessary.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis. Which management principle is most appropriate?

choices.text: Withhold all TB treatment until after breastfeeding
Discharge her without follow-up because pregnancy protects against TB
Link her promptly to TB services for appropriate treatment and infection-control counselling
Treat her only with antimalarial medication

questions.rationale: Active TB in pregnancy requires prompt treatment with an appropriate regimen under national TB guidance. Delaying treatment can harm both mother and fetus, while infection-control measures reduce transmission to household members and newborns.

questions.question_text: Which hormone is primarily responsible for increasing insulin resistance during pregnancy?

choices.text: Human placental lactogen
Oxytocin
Prolactin alone
Melatonin

questions.rationale: Human placental lactogen contributes to maternal insulin resistance as pregnancy progresses. This adaptation helps make more glucose available to the fetus but can contribute to gestational diabetes in susceptible women.

questions.question_text: A woman with poorly controlled gestational diabetes is at increased risk of delivering an infant with which complication?

choices.text: Low birth weight in every case
Macrosomia
Congenital absence of the placenta
Neonatal dehydration in every case

questions.rationale: Maternal hyperglycaemia can cause fetal hyperinsulinaemia and excessive fetal growth, resulting in macrosomia. This increases the risk of birth trauma, shoulder dystocia and operative delivery.

questions.question_text: A woman with gestational diabetes has repeated fasting blood glucose readings above her treatment targets despite dietary modification and physical activity. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Advise her to stop monitoring blood glucose
Tell her that medication is never used during pregnancy
Refer or escalate for review of glycaemic control and possible pharmacological treatment
Recommend fasting throughout the day

questions.rationale: Persistent hyperglycaemia despite lifestyle intervention requires clinical review and possible pharmacological treatment, commonly insulin where indicated. Poor glycaemic control increases the risk of maternal and fetal complications.

questions.question_text: Which finding is commonly associated with untreated maternal hyperthyroidism?

choices.text: Persistent bradycardia and cold intolerance
Reduced metabolic activity in all body systems
Severe constipation as the only clinical feature
Tachycardia, heat intolerance, tremor and weight loss

questions.rationale: Hyperthyroidism increases metabolic activity and may cause tachycardia, tremor, heat intolerance and weight loss. Uncontrolled disease during pregnancy can cause serious maternal and fetal complications.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with Graves' disease develops high fever, severe tachycardia, agitation and vomiting. Which emergency should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Thyroid storm
Uncomplicated morning sickness
Physiological anaemia
Normal labour onset

questions.rationale: Thyroid storm is a life-threatening exacerbation of thyrotoxicosis characterised by severe systemic symptoms such as fever, tachycardia and altered mental status. Immediate emergency treatment and specialist management are required.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with known hypothyroidism asks whether she should stop levothyroxine because she is pregnant. What is the best advice?

choices.text: Stop levothyroxine immediately after a positive pregnancy test
Continue treatment and arrange prompt thyroid function monitoring and dose review by the managing clinician
Replace levothyroxine with iron tablets
Take levothyroxine only when symptoms occur

questions.rationale: Levothyroxine is important for maintaining maternal thyroid hormone levels and supporting fetal development. Requirements may increase during pregnancy, so thyroid function should be monitored and the dose adjusted by the managing clinician when necessary.

questions.question_text: A woman with type 1 diabetes is admitted with vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing and marked hyperglycaemia. What condition should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Hypothyroidism
Uncomplicated gastro-oesophageal reflux
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Physiological nausea of pregnancy

questions.rationale: Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing and hyperglycaemia suggest diabetic ketoacidosis, which can develop at lower glucose levels in pregnancy than outside pregnancy. It is a medical emergency requiring urgent hospital treatment and close maternal and fetal monitoring.

questions.question_text: Which renal change normally occurs during pregnancy?

choices.text: Increased renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate
Complete cessation of urine production
Permanent obstruction of both ureters
A universal reduction in renal blood flow

questions.rationale: Renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate increase during normal pregnancy. These physiological changes influence the interpretation of renal function tests and fluid balance.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 24 weeks presents with fever, flank pain, vomiting and tenderness at the costovertebral angle. What condition should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Uncomplicated vaginal candidiasis
Acute pyelonephritis
Physiological urinary frequency
Gestational diabetes without complications

questions.rationale: Fever, flank pain, vomiting and costovertebral angle tenderness are suggestive of acute pyelonephritis. Pregnancy-associated pyelonephritis can cause maternal sepsis and requires urgent clinical assessment and appropriate antibiotic treatment.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with suspected pyelonephritis becomes hypotensive, confused and tachycardic. What is the priority action?

choices.text: Arrange routine urine testing at the next antenatal visit
Encourage oral fluids and send her home
Recognise possible sepsis, initiate emergency assessment and arrange urgent hospital management
Advise her to stop all prescribed medicines

questions.rationale: Hypotension, confusion and tachycardia suggest possible sepsis with organ dysfunction. Immediate escalation, resuscitation and prompt antimicrobial treatment are essential.

questions.question_text: Which finding is most suggestive of significant renal impairment in a pregnant woman?

choices.text: Mild urinary frequency without other symptoms
Increased appetite during pregnancy
Normal physiological ankle swelling alone
Persistent oliguria with rising serum creatinine

questions.rationale: Persistent oliguria and rising serum creatinine suggest impaired renal function. These findings require prompt assessment because renal impairment during pregnancy may be associated with severe maternal complications.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with chronic kidney disease develops worsening hypertension, proteinuria and declining renal function. What should the midwife consider?

choices.text: Possible progression of renal disease or superimposed pre-eclampsia requiring specialist assessment
Normal changes that never require follow-up
An indication to stop all antenatal care
A definite diagnosis of gestational diabetes

questions.rationale: Worsening hypertension, proteinuria and renal function in a woman with chronic kidney disease may indicate disease progression or superimposed pre-eclampsia. Specialist assessment is needed to distinguish the causes and guide maternal and fetal management.

questions.question_text: Why is pregnancy associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism?

choices.text: Pregnancy causes permanent destruction of all platelets
Pregnancy produces a hypercoagulable state, venous stasis and changes in vascular function
Pregnancy prevents blood clot formation
Pregnancy causes complete absence of circulating clotting factors

questions.rationale: Pregnancy increases the risk of venous thromboembolism through hypercoagulability, venous stasis and vascular changes. The risk is particularly important in the postpartum period.

questions.question_text: A woman at 29 weeks' gestation presents with unilateral calf swelling, warmth, redness and pain. Which condition should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Bilateral physiological ankle oedema
Normal pregnancy-related weight gain
Deep vein thrombosis
Uncomplicated varicose veins without symptoms

questions.rationale: Unilateral swelling, warmth, redness and pain are concerning features of deep vein thrombosis. Urgent diagnostic assessment is required because an untreated thrombus may lead to pulmonary embolism.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with suspected deep vein thrombosis suddenly develops chest pain, severe breathlessness and oxygen desaturation. What should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Pulmonary embolism
Uncomplicated gastro-oesophageal reflux
Normal physiological breathlessness
Iron-deficiency anaemia alone

questions.rationale: Sudden chest pain, dyspnoea and hypoxaemia in a woman with suspected DVT strongly suggest pulmonary embolism. This is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate resuscitation and urgent specialist management.

questions.question_text: Which anticoagulant is commonly preferred for the treatment of venous thromboembolism during pregnancy?

choices.text: Warfarin throughout pregnancy
Aspirin as the sole treatment for acute DVT
Oral vitamin K
Low-molecular-weight heparin

questions.rationale: Low-molecular-weight heparin is commonly used for treating venous thromboembolism during pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta. Treatment and timing around delivery require specialist planning and monitoring.

questions.question_text: A woman receiving anticoagulant therapy for DVT asks whether she should stop treatment because she is approaching delivery. What is the best response?

choices.text: Stop anticoagulation without informing the clinical team
Continue or adjust treatment according to an individualised specialist delivery and anticoagulation plan
Replace anticoagulation with herbal preparations
Double the dose during labour

questions.rationale: Anticoagulation around delivery requires individualised planning to balance thrombosis and bleeding risks. The woman should not stop or alter treatment independently but should follow the coordinated obstetric and haematology plan.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial approach to a pregnant woman who collapses and is unresponsive?

choices.text: Assess responsiveness, summon emergency assistance and assess airway, breathing and circulation
Begin routine antenatal history-taking
Give oral fluids immediately
Wait for a relative to arrive before assessing her

questions.rationale: An unresponsive pregnant woman requires immediate emergency assessment using a structured approach to airway, breathing and circulation. Resuscitation should begin promptly, with pregnancy-specific modifications and emergency support as appropriate.

questions.question_text: A woman at 36 weeks' gestation collapses from cardiac arrest. Which modification is essential during maternal cardiopulmonary resuscitation?

choices.text: Avoid chest compressions because of the pregnancy
Perform compressions only after delivery of the baby
Use manual left uterine displacement when the uterus is large enough to cause aortocaval compression
Place the woman in a fully upright sitting position for compressions

questions.rationale: Manual left uterine displacement helps relieve aortocaval compression and improve venous return during maternal resuscitation. High-quality chest compressions and standard advanced life support measures must not be delayed.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman develops sudden severe breathlessness, hypotension and cyanosis shortly after delivery. What is the most appropriate response?

choices.text: Treat the event as a possible life-threatening cardiopulmonary emergency and initiate immediate resuscitation and specialist escalation
Assume it is normal postpartum fatigue
Encourage her to walk to improve circulation
Delay intervention until a routine chest X-ray is performed

questions.rationale: Sudden respiratory distress and cardiovascular collapse after delivery may indicate pulmonary embolism, amniotic fluid embolism or another critical condition. Immediate resuscitation and multidisciplinary emergency management are essential.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with severe vomiting is unable to retain fluids and has signs of dehydration and ketonuria. Which condition should the midwife consider?

choices.text: Normal mild morning sickness
Hyperemesis gravidarum
Uncomplicated gestational hypertension
Physiological urinary frequency

questions.rationale: Persistent severe vomiting with dehydration and ketonuria suggests hyperemesis gravidarum. The woman may require hospital assessment, fluid and electrolyte correction, antiemetic treatment and nutritional support.

questions.question_text: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia receiving magnesium sulphate has a respiratory rate of 8 breaths per minute and absent deep tendon reflexes. Which action should be prioritised?

choices.text: Increase the infusion rate to prevent further seizures
Encourage oral fluids and continue treatment
Stop magnesium sulphate, call for urgent assistance and prepare calcium gluconate according to protocol
Allow the woman to sleep and reassess in two hours

questions.rationale: Respiratory depression and absent reflexes are signs of magnesium sulphate toxicity. The infusion must be stopped, urgent support provided and calcium gluconate prepared as the antidote according to the clinical protocol.

questions.question_text: A woman with diabetes in pregnancy becomes unconscious, and her blood glucose is found to be severely low. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

choices.text: Give oral glucose gel or sweetened water despite her unconscious state
Administer her usual insulin dose
Wait until she regains consciousness without intervention
Protect her airway and administer appropriate emergency glucose treatment according to protocol

questions.rationale: Severe hypoglycaemia with unconsciousness is a medical emergency. Oral fluids must not be given because of aspiration risk; intravenous glucose or glucagon should be administered according to the emergency protocol.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with severe hypertension complains of sudden severe headache, develops weakness on one side of her body and has difficulty speaking. Which complication should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Stroke
Uncomplicated tension headache
Normal pregnancy-related fatigue
Mild dehydration

questions.rationale: Sudden focal neurological deficits and severe headache may indicate stroke, a life-threatening complication of severe hypertension and pre-eclampsia. Immediate emergency assessment and referral for definitive management are required.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman presents at a district hospital with severe vaginal bleeding, pallor, cold clammy skin and a weak rapid pulse. Which action should the midwife take first?

choices.text: Complete routine registration before initiating care
Activate the emergency response, assess ABCs and initiate resuscitation while arranging urgent obstetric management
Ask the woman to walk to the laboratory
Give oral iron tablets and observe her overnight

questions.rationale: The findings indicate haemorrhagic shock and require immediate emergency management. Resuscitation, intravenous access, blood preparation and urgent identification and control of the bleeding source must proceed without delay.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman with suspected pulmonary embolism becomes unresponsive and has no normal breathing. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Wait for confirmation by imaging before starting treatment
Place her in a sitting position and observe
Start cardiopulmonary resuscitation, activate the emergency response and follow advanced life support procedures
Administer oral anticoagulants immediately

questions.rationale: Cardiac arrest requires immediate high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation and activation of the emergency response. Diagnostic imaging must not delay resuscitation or time-critical advanced life support.

questions.question_text: A woman with chronic hypertension is attending antenatal clinic. Which finding should prompt urgent assessment for possible superimposed pre-eclampsia?

choices.text: A mild increase in appetite
Normal fetal movements
Occasional painless fetal hiccups
New severe headache, visual disturbance and worsening blood pressure

questions.rationale: New neurological symptoms and worsening hypertension in a woman with chronic hypertension raise concern for superimposed pre-eclampsia. Urgent maternal assessment, laboratory investigations and fetal evaluation are required.

questions.question_text: A woman at 28 weeks' gestation with severe malaria develops jaundice, respiratory distress and reduced urine output. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.text: She has uncomplicated malaria suitable for routine outpatient treatment
She may have severe malaria with multi-organ involvement and requires urgent hospital management
The symptoms are normal physiological changes of pregnancy
She should discontinue all treatment until delivery

questions.rationale: Jaundice, respiratory distress and reduced urine output indicate possible severe malaria with organ dysfunction. Immediate emergency treatment, close monitoring and specialist care are necessary to reduce maternal and fetal mortality.
